EU–UK summit: a “historic” deal on food, carbon and 100,000 young people, but everything hinges on university fees

Meeting in Brussels on Friday 20 November, Andy Burnham and EU leaders concluded three agreements: checks on food products, youth mobility and the carbon market. But Brussels will only apply them once there is a deal on the fees European students pay in the UK, which has been pushed back six months [1][2].
The second EU–UK summit since Brexit ended on Friday in Brussels with a series of agreements covering food and agricultural standards, carbon markets and mobility [4].
The food component eases checks on food exports; the carbon component links the emissions trading systems [9][1].

The mobility scheme could open the UK to 100,000 young Europeans coming to work there temporarily [3]. The draft text aims for implementation “by 2028 at the latest” and places open to young people “by January 2030 at the latest” [2].

The sticking point: university fees. Today, a European student in the UK pays the international rate, several times what a British student pays [1]. Brussels wants equal treatment; London is offering a smaller reduction [4].

The two sides have given themselves six months to agree on this point, and the 27 member states have made it known that they will freeze implementation of the three agreements until then; the EU is aiming for a start on 1 March 2028 [1].

“The deal is done, the negotiations are over,” Downing Street said [8]. Andy Burnham spoke of “a good day for Britain” and “for Europe”, and said he wanted to repair some of the damage done by “hard Brexit”; these agreements had been launched by his predecessor Keir Starmer [1][3].
In the UK, Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, accused the Prime Minister of “betraying” Brexit [7].

Key takeaway: this is the clearest rapprochement between London and the EU since the UK left in 2020, as the leaked draft conclusions had suggested [5]. But it is above all a timetable, not yet rules in force [1].

University fees have become Brussels’ lever: by tying the three agreements to this issue, the Europeans gain leverage on a subject London wanted to keep separate [1]. On the British side, bringing fees for Europeans into line with those for British students would deprive universities of part of their revenue, hence London’s more limited offer [4].

The summit leaves other issues open, in particular the UK’s access to the European electricity market [4][5]. Andy Burnham acknowledges that the “sector-by-sector” approach is reaching its limits and says he is exploring more ambitious options [4]; he had announced a national consultation on the long-term relationship with the EU after the summit, at a time when he was admitting that Brexit’s promises had failed [6].
Politically, it is a risky bet: Reform UK is turning this rapprochement into a campaign argument against the Labour government [7].

If you are between 18 and 30, this scheme could one day let you work for a few months in the UK without a standard work visa, but not before 2028 at the earliest. If you are thinking of studying across the Channel, fees for now remain those of an international student: keep an eye on the outcome of the negotiations over the next six months.

news.2026-11-21-canada-trump-enhardi-def: Ottawa, Canada
Canada
Canada: Trump calls Ottawa “emboldened” and only wants real talks once the US trade deficit is at zero, while a Democratic senator advises signing an interim deal

On Friday 20 November, Donald Trump said he was working on a “fair” deal with Canada, while calling the country “emboldened” and making real talks conditional on a zero trade deficit. The day before, the House of Commons had passed Mark Carney’s budget by 162 votes to 151 [1][2][5].

At his White House press conference, Donald Trump said: “We are working on a deal that is fair,” adding that there was still work to do [1]. He said Canada felt “emboldened” and repeated that the country was taking advantage of the United States [2].

He said he was ready to talk once the US trade deficit with Canada had fallen to zero [2]. He puts it at around $80 billion; official US figures for 2025 show $48 billion in goods, mainly due to purchases of Canadian energy, according to The Canadian Press [2].

He described Mark Carney as “very nice” after their exchange on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen [2]. Negotiations stalled in August, and since then Washington has imposed 50% tariffs on many Canadian products [2].

Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc acknowledges that an interim deal would probably keep “232” tariffs on steel, aluminium, cars and softwood lumber, at lower rates [3]. In his view, easing these tariffs and the “338” tariffs would make it possible to open the formal review of the North American agreement (CUSMA) [3].

Democratic Senator Chris Coons (Delaware) advised Ottawa on CBC to accept an interim deal if one is possible, then let the future Democratic majority in Congress “legislate” a better deal [4]. He believes removing the “338” tariffs would be a major step forward and calls the “232” tariffs an “insult” to Canada [4].

On Thursday 19 November, the House of Commons passed the 2026 budget by 162 votes to 151, with the entire opposition voting against [5][6]. It forecasts a deficit of C$62.3 billion; Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne insists that “confident countries invest” [5].

Key takeaway: Ottawa is seeking a tariff truce before the end of the year, but Donald Trump has set a condition, a zero trade deficit, that Canada cannot meet quickly since it mainly sells oil to the United States [2][3].

Canada is therefore playing on two fronts: it is negotiating with Washington while signing more and more agreements in Asia. “If the United States doesn’t want a deal, we’re busy,” Mark Carney had said; he hopes for a free trade agreement with India within three months [7].
The Democratic victory in Congress changes the calculation: for Chris Coons, an interim deal is enough, as the rest could go through legislation from January [4].
Domestically, the budget vote strengthens Mark Carney’s government, even though the implementing legislation still has to pass [5].

Canada is a key partner of the European Union, with which it is drawing closer to reduce its dependence on the United States. The longer the North American trade war lasts, the more Ottawa looks for outlets elsewhere, including in Europe: this could open markets to French companies, but also bring more Canadian competition.

news.2026-11-21-irak-jurf-al-sakhar-kata: Jurf al-Sakhar, Iraq
Iraq
Iraq: the army enters the stronghold of the pro-Iranian militia Kataeb Hezbollah, accused of stealing state oil

On Friday 20 November, Iraq’s federal police and army began taking control of Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad, held since 2014 by the Kataeb Hezbollah militia, an ally of Iran. A compromise negotiated the day before averted a confrontation, but the militia’s complete withdrawal remains uncertain [1][2][4].

On Friday, federal police units and other forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar, in Babil province, under a compromise with Kataeb Hezbollah [1][2]. According to the official INA news agency, a control headquarters has been set up there and the federal police are taking charge of the site [4].

This joint command reports to the federal police (Interior Ministry) and brings together the army and units of the Popular Mobilisation Forces [4][5]. An army brigade, a federal police battalion and an energy police regiment will protect the oil pipelines, and the road is due to reopen to civilians [5].

The compromise was announced on Thursday 19 November by three senior security officials, according to Reuters: Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had prepared his troops to go in by force. Senior Shiite political leaders acted as mediators, and Esmail Qaani, head of the Quds Force of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, came to Baghdad to calm things down [3].

A government spokesperson said the new headquarters had been operating since 20 November, the day of the ultimatum given to the militia; according to a source quoted by The National, the Prime Minister agreed to avoid any direct confrontation [2][3].

At the root of the crisis is oil: according to Reuters sources, a smuggling network operating from Jurf al-Sakhar, with accomplices among security and oil officials, has cost the state hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021. Nine senior officials have been dismissed [7].

Kataeb Hezbollah denies any smuggling and claims the operation is aimed at disarming it; the militia had mobilised around 8,000 fighters from several provinces towards Jurf al-Sakhar, according to Reuters [7].

Key takeaway: for the first time in more than ten years, the Iraqi state is regaining a foothold in an area that the most powerful militia allied with Tehran treated as its own territory, and it is doing so without a fight [1][6].

Jurf al-Sakhar, renamed Jurf al-Nasr, has been controlled by Kataeb Hezbollah since it was retaken from the Islamic State group in October 2014 [6]. Residents have never been able to return, and the site had become a base closed to the authorities [6].

The compromise remains fragile. The militia’s withdrawal is “uncertain”, writes Asharq Al-Awsat [4]. According to Iraqi News, one wing of the group, that of Al-Hamidawi, has proposed postponing any handover of the site until 30 June 2027 [8].

The stakes are also economic: Baghdad wants to show it can protect its oil pipelines and oil revenue, at a time when Iran, at war with the United States, is keen to keep its armed allies in the region [3][7].

Iraq is one of the Gulf’s major oil exporters. If Baghdad manages to shut off the smuggling and placate its militias without a battle, that is one less risk for crude supply, already disrupted by the war around Hormuz, and therefore for what you pay to fill up your tank.

Somalia: Mogadishu gives the UAE ambassador 72 hours to leave and denounces an “open invasion” through the ports

On Thursday 19 November, the Somali government ordered the ambassador of the United Arab Emirates to leave the country within 72 hours and recalled its own ambassador. It accuses Abu Dhabi of port agreements signed without its consent in Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo. The UAE denounces a “hostile” approach [1][2][3][5].
On Thursday, the Somali Council of Ministers decided to expel the Emirati ambassador, with a 72-hour deadline, and to recall the Somali ambassador in Abu Dhabi [2][5].

Information Minister Abdifatah Kasim Mohamud spoke of an “open invasion” and warned that “measures will be taken against anyone who cooperates with the UAE in the invasion of Somalia” [1][4]. He did not specify which actions by the UAE had triggered the decision [1].

Two days earlier, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud had accused Abu Dhabi of interfering in the country’s affairs and undermining its unity by signing port agreements in Berbera and Bosaso, in the north, and in Kismayo, in the south, without the federal government’s approval [1].

On Friday, the Emirati Foreign Ministry condemned Mogadishu’s “escalatory and hostile approach”, accusing it of dragging the UAE into its internal power struggles [3]. Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the Emirati president, described the Somali remarks as an “attack” that “reflects the shifting nature of its positions” [3].

Relations had already broken down in practice: in January 2026, Somalia cancelled all its agreements with the UAE, including on ports, security and defence [1][6]. Mogadishu had then accused Abu Dhabi of illegally bringing the Yemeni separatist Aidarous al-Zubaidi in through Somaliland [6].

The UAE denies any interference [1]. In January, the Emirati operator DP World said the port of Berbera was continuing to operate under existing agreements [7]; it had pledged to invest $442 million there [8].
Key takeaway: Somalia is moving from a quarrel to a diplomatic break with the UAE, one of the Gulf powers most present in the Horn of Africa, at the entrance to the Red Sea [1][2].

At the heart of the conflict are the ports. Abu Dhabi deals directly with Somali regions, such as Somaliland, which claims independence, or with federal member states, to control ports on the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Mogadishu sees this as an attack on its sovereignty [1][6].

It is also a domestic crisis. Puntland and Jubaland, which are close to the UAE, oppose the federal government over constitutional changes and the organisation of the next elections [6]. By expelling the ambassador, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud is also targeting these rivals; Abu Dhabi accuses him of exporting his internal disputes [3].

These Somali ports line the shipping route between Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, the one used by a large share of the goods you buy. The more unstable the region, the more expensive shipping becomes and the longer delivery times get.

Costa Rica: President Laura Fernández, who says she has received death threats from prisons, refuses to release $67 million to the judiciary amid a crisis between the branches of power

On Friday 20 November, Costa Rican President Laura Fernández met the presidents of the Supreme Court, the Legislative Assembly and the electoral tribunal. They pledged to act together against organised crime, but remain divided over 30 billion colones ($67 million) of the judicial budget that the executive is blocking [1][2].
The 20 November meeting brought together Laura Fernández, Patricia Vargas (Supreme Court), Yara Jiménez (Legislative Assembly) and Eugenia Zamora (Supreme Electoral Tribunal) [1].
They decided to set up a working group so that the police can access information on arrest warrants more easily [1]. But disagreement persists over the judiciary’s budget for 2027 [1].

Laura Fernández defends the restrictions imposed on around 30,000 million colones ($67 million) of this budget and rules out negotiating “out of goodwill”: she prefers to wait for the ruling of the constitutional chamber, which has received challenges against these measures [2].

On 16 November, she said that criminal organisations had ordered her assassination from prisons, and defended the new high-security centre for organised crime inmates (CACCO) [3]. On 10 November, she had met the US DEA and the US embassy after a record seizure of 74 tonnes of drugs [4].

On the economic front, she appointed First Vice-President Francisco Gamboa as Minister of Foreign Trade, effective 20 November, following the departure of Indiana Trejos [5]. On 28 October, she had announced that Costa Rica was abandoning its bid to join the Trans-Pacific agreement (CPTPP), a decision taken at least six days earlier, according to the presidency [6].

In her 15 November address on the “jaguar economy”, she said Costa Rica would grow faster than the rest of Latin America; the outlet CRHoy notes that the central bank forecasts a slowdown and that average household income fell by 3.8% in 2026 [7].
Key takeaway: in Costa Rica, the executive and the judiciary are clashing over money and over how to fight organised crime [1][2].

The record seizure of 74 tonnes of drugs and the death threats against the president show the power of criminal networks, and for Laura Fernández they justify a hard line in cooperation with Washington [3][4].

The budget standoff raises a question of separation of powers: by blocking $67 million in judicial funding, the executive puts pressure on judges who oversee its actions, and it is the constitutional chamber that will have to decide [2].
Abandoning the Trans-Pacific agreement and changing the Minister of Foreign Trade also signal a shift in trade policy [5][6].

Costa Rica is a popular destination for French travellers. The rise of organised crime and the crisis between the branches of power have no immediate effect on you, but if you are planning to travel there, check the travel advice from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

news.2026-11-21-vallourec-chute-bourse.t: Vallourec plunges 14.6% in Paris: the war in the Middle East more than halves its profit and pushes the recovery back to 2027
news.2026-11-21-vallourec-chute-bourse.s: On Friday 20 November, shares in the French maker of steel tubes for oil and gas fell 14.57%, to their lowest level in 150 sessions. The cause: a 56% drop in quarterly profit, weighed down by extra transport costs in the Middle East, and a year-end forecast well below expectations [1][5][6].
news.2026-11-21-vallourec-chute-bourse.p: In the third quarter, net profit attributable to the group fell to $66 million, from $152 million a year earlier, and revenue dropped 10% to $956 million [3].

EBITDA (what the business earns before depreciation and financial costs) fell 26% year on year, for a margin of 18.9% [4]. At $181 million, however, it was almost in line with the $183 million expected by analysts, according to Investing.com [2].

What sent the shares tumbling was the outlook: Vallourec is targeting EBITDA of $170 million to $210 million in the fourth quarter. The midpoint of this range is 25% below the Visible Alpha consensus of $253 million, according to calculations by the bank Jefferies [2].

CEO Philippe Guillemot attributes the decline to additional costs in the Middle East, linked to the war’s logistical disruptions, which will be “largely reimbursed” in the coming quarters, and to a disruption at a subcontractor in the United States [4][7].
For the whole of 2026, the group is maintaining an EBITDA target of $760 million to $800 million [4].
At the close, the shares had lost 14.57%, one of the biggest falls of the session in Paris, on a day when the CAC 40 shed 1.89% [5]. They broke below their 150-session lows [6].

The broker TP ICAP Midcap believes the improvement expected at the end of the year has been pushed back to 2027 [1]. The website Upside24 also points out that the third quarter of 2025 had been boosted by the sale of the subsidiary Serimax [8].
news.2026-11-21-vallourec-chute-bourse.w: Key takeaway: on the stock market, you buy the future. The past quarter was roughly in line; it was the forecast for the next quarter, much lower than expected, that drove investors away [2].

Vallourec is a barometer of the oil industry: its tubes are used to drill oil and gas wells, notably in the Middle East. The war is not only pushing up crude prices: it is disrupting the transport of goods and making deliveries more expensive, which eats into margins [3][7].
The group plans to gradually pass some of these extra costs on to its customers [2]. If it succeeds, margins could recover in 2027; if not, the promised rebound risks slipping further.
news.2026-11-21-vallourec-chute-bourse.f: Vallourec is an SBF 120 stock often held in French equity funds and PEA accounts. The session shows that a French company can be hit hard by a distant war, not by missiles, but by the cost of transport.

news.2026-11-21-vallourec-chute-bourse.d: How it works: why a forecast matters more than a result

A share price reflects what investors think the company will earn in the years ahead. Analysts publish forecasts, whose average forms the “consensus”. When a company announces a target well below it, here 25% below the consensus for the fourth quarter [2], investors suddenly revise all their calculations downwards, and the share price adjusts within minutes. A quarter in line with expectations, like Vallourec’s [2], does not make up for bad news about what comes next.
news.2026-11-21-vallourec-chute-bourse.p: Precedents: Vallourec, a stock used to upheavals
At the end of a financial restructuring, Vallourec raised €300 million by issuing shares at €5.66; the stock fell nearly 8% to €8.29, according to Option Finance [9].
Creating many new shares dilutes existing shareholders: each one holds a smaller slice of the pie.
The group announced it had completed its financial restructuring, after years of losses [10].
Today’s Vallourec is a company relieved of its debts; comparing its share price before and after 2021 makes no sense.
In the second quarter, EBITDA fell 9% to $190 million, and the group was cautious because of the war in the Middle East [11]; it paid an exceptional interim dividend of €2.05 per share [12].
The warning about the Middle East dated back to the summer: the market was expecting a recovery at the end of the year, which is not happening.

news.2026-11-21-italie-greve-generale-cg: Italy: general strike against Meloni’s budget, the CGIL union claims 1.5 million demonstrators

On Friday 20 November, Italy’s largest union, the CGIL, held a 24-hour general strike against Giorgia Meloni’s government’s 2027 budget. The union claims 1.5 million people took part in more than 100 cities [1][3].
The strike covered the entire public and private sectors, from schools to healthcare and buses, but not trains or planes; a separate rail strike ran from 9 pm on Friday to 8 pm on Saturday [1].

The CGIL reports a 60% strike turnout and 1.5 million demonstrators, figures not confirmed by an independent source [3]. In Rome, Maurizio Landini, its general secretary, spoke of “well over a million” people [4].
In Rome, firecrackers were thrown at the Education Ministry and tensions flared in Turin [4]. Minister Giuseppe Valditara called the violence “serious” [6].
Maurizio Landini repeats that “the budget must change” [2] and threatens a rally outside Parliament if it is not amended [6].

Key takeaway: the street is putting pressure on the Italian budget at a time when the government is still discussing its most costly items: pensions, healthcare and the “Superbonus” tax credits for home renovation [5].
Giorgia Meloni has already agreed to withdraw a contested measure on schools, but Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti refuses to touch the overall balance of the text [5].
If you are travelling in Italy in the coming days, check for transport strikes. More broadly, this standoff shows how hard it is to fix public finances without cutting services.

news.2026-11-21-chili-kast-japon-takaich: Chile: in Tokyo, José Antonio Kast offers Japan his country’s critical minerals, as China has cut off rare earths to the Japanese

On Friday 20 November in Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received Chilean President José Antonio Kast, followed by Peru’s Keiko Fujimori. On the agenda: critical minerals, defence and investment [1][2][3].

Japan has been looking for other rare earth suppliers since China cut off its exports to the archipelago in January [1]. Tokyo also wants to strengthen its defence cooperation with Chile, which would pave the way for equipment exports, according to Nikkei Asia [3].
Kast invited Sanae Takaichi to Chile for the 130th anniversary of diplomatic relations in 2027, and invited Japanese companies to the “Choose Chile” summit in March 2027 [2].
Addressing Japanese business leaders, he said: “You bring the capital, and together we will become famous,” while touting a cut in corporate tax [4].

Key takeaway: by receiving Chile and Peru on the same day, Tokyo is looking in South America for minerals that do not depend on Beijing, and Santiago is positioning itself as a partner, including on defence [1][3].
Kast, whose approval rating has fallen to 18% according to a recent poll, is betting on foreign investment: the central bank forecasts only 0.25% to 0.75% growth in 2026 [5][6].
South American copper and lithium end up in the batteries and electric cars sold in Europe: the race between countries for these suppliers weighs on their prices.

news.2026-11-21-suisse-udc-aeschi-graber: Switzerland: to succeed Guy Parmelin in government, the SVP picks two German speakers and sidelines the French speakers

On Friday 20 November, the parliamentary group of the SVP (conservative right) nominated Thomas Aeschi from Zug and Michael Graber from Upper Valais to succeed minister Guy Parmelin on the Federal Council, the Swiss government. Parliament will elect the new minister on 9 December [1][2].
Thomas Aeschi was nominated first, with 37 votes after six rounds; Michael Graber followed in the seventh round, with 42 votes [1][2].
Eight candidates were in the running, including two French speakers, Céline Amaudruz and Pierre Alain Schnegg: neither is on the final “ticket” [3][4].
Thomas Aeschi highlights fifteen years in the National Council and nine years as head of the SVP group [5].
The Greens refuse to hold hearings with the two candidates, whom they consider “unelectable” [1][2].

Key takeaway: barring a surprise, Guy Parmelin, who announced his departure in early October, will be replaced by a German speaker, and neither of the two French-speaking candidates got through their party’s filter [6][1][3].

In Switzerland, Parliament elects each minister, and in theory it can choose someone other than a party’s official candidates; hence the importance of the hearings held by the other groups before 9 December [1][2].

Switzerland is an important neighbour and economic partner of France. The political make-up of its government affects its relations with the European Union, and therefore the rules that apply on both sides of the border.

news.2026-11-21-georgie-tbilissi-explosi: Georgia: a gas explosion rips open a Tbilisi apartment building, six dead including two children, national mourning this Sunday

On Thursday 19 November, a gas leak caused the partial collapse of an apartment building in the Ponichala district of Tbilisi. Six people died, including two minors, and five were injured. The government has declared national mourning on 22 November [1][2][3].
The explosion destroyed part of the building; a gas heater is believed to have caused it, according to the authorities [1][2].
Rescuers pulled a 3-year-old child alive from the rubble, whose life is not in danger; Interior Minister Soulkhan Tamazashvili declared the search practically over [1].
Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze says 28 of the nearly 90 families in the building have been rehoused in hotels [1].
Flags will fly at half-mast throughout the country on Sunday 22 November [4].
Key takeaway: the tragedy revives the question of the safety of gas installations in old apartment buildings, at the start of winter, when heaters are running at full blast [1][2].

For the city authorities, the immediate challenge is rehousing: more than 60 families from the building had not yet been rehoused in hotels at the time of the update [1]. The government chose national mourning, a sign of the emotion felt across the country [4].
This tragedy is a reminder of a useful habit at home too: have your gas boiler or heater checked every year and install a carbon monoxide detector, especially at the start of winter.
news.2026-11-21-equateur-noboa-campagne-: Ecuador: Daniel Noboa steps away from the presidency again to campaign, eight days before local elections brought forward by two and a half months

Since Friday 20 November, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa has been on leave from his office to support his party ADN’s candidates in the 29 November local elections. The vote, brought forward from 14 February 2027, is seen as a test a year after his referendum defeat [1][2][3].
On 29 November, Ecuadorians will elect prefects, mayors, municipal councillors, members of parish councils and of the Council for Citizen Participation and Social Control (CPCCS) [1].
The National Electoral Council (CNE) brought forward the vote, originally scheduled for 14 February 2027 [1].

Daniel Noboa obtained two periods of leave to campaign, from 12 to 18 and then from 20 to 26 November; he returned to the presidency for a single day, 19 November, according to the Venezuelan agency AVN [1][2].
In November 2025, the “no” vote won on all four questions of his referendum, including the return of foreign military bases [3].
Key takeaway: these local elections will show whether Daniel Noboa has regained voters’ support after his referendum setback, something analysts are watching closely [1][3].

The stakes go beyond town halls: security, in the face of drug-trafficking gangs, and the relationship with Washington, complicated by the rejection of foreign bases, remain at the heart of his term [3].
Ecuador is a major exporter of bananas and shrimp to Europe. A political or security crisis could weigh on these sectors, with no immediate effect on your shopping.
